lessons.title: Preparing for health care work
lessons.html:
Preparing for health care work

This practical module is about doing health care tasks correctly and safely: examining animals, giving remedies, treating wounds and dipping. Good preparation prevents most mistakes and injuries.

Before you start

  1. Know the task. Get the instruction from your supervisor or the vet's treatment sheet: which animals, which product, what dose, which route.
  2. Read the label. Check the species, dose per kilogram, route, storage, protective clothing and withdrawal period. Check the expiry date.
  3. Check the facilities. The kraal, race and crush must be in working order. Gates must close, the head clamp must work and there must be no sharp wire or bolts sticking out.
  4. Get the equipment ready. Dosing gun, syringes and needles of the right size, thermometer, marking crayon or spray, scale or weigh band, record sheet and pen, cooler box for vaccines.
  5. Wear protective clothing. Overalls, boots, gloves and eye protection as the label requires.

Handling vaccines

Many vaccines must be kept cold. Keep them in the fridge, carry them to the kraal in a cooler box out of the sun, and only draw up what you will use soon. Do not mix vaccines in one syringe unless the label says you may. Dispose of opened live vaccines as the label instructs.

Restraint

Bring animals in quietly. Use the crush for cattle; catch sheep and goats against the side of a small pen and hold them firmly, not by the wool. Never put your arm through the bars of the crush in front of a moving animal. Make sure someone is with you when working with cattle.

lessons.title: Examining animals and giving remedies
lessons.html:
Examining animals and giving remedies

A quick examination

  • Take the rectal temperature with a clean thermometer; hold the thermometer so it is not lost.
  • Look at the eyes, gums and eyelids for colour; use the FAMACHA chart for sheep and goats if trained.
  • Check the nose, breathing, dung and skin.
  • Feel body condition over the back and ribs.
  • Look at the feet, udder and any swellings.
  • Record the tag number and what you found, and report to your supervisor.

Dosing by mouth

Calibrate the dosing gun to the dose on the label for the animal's weight. Dose the heaviest animals in the group at the correct weight rather than underdosing - underdosing builds worm resistance. Insert the nozzle gently from the side of the mouth over the tongue and squeeze slowly. Never dose an animal with its head held high or lying on its back; liquid can go into the lungs.

Injections

RouteWhere (follow label)
Subcutaneous (under the skin)Loose skin of the neck or behind the shoulder
Intramuscular (into muscle)Neck muscle, as the label directs

Use the needle size and site the label or vet gives. Use the neck rather than the rump for cattle to avoid damaging valuable meat cuts. Change needles regularly and whenever they become blunt or dirty. Never recap needles by hand; put used needles in a sharps container.

Pour-ons and sprays

Apply along the back line as the label says, at the correct dose for weight. Do not apply to wet animals unless the label allows it.

After treatment

Mark treated animals, record date, product, batch, dose and withdrawal date, clean equipment and store remedies safely.

lessons.title: Wound care, dipping and hoof care
lessons.html:
Wound care, dipping and hoof care

Treating wounds

  1. Restrain the animal safely.
  2. Wearing gloves, clean the wound with clean water and a mild antiseptic. Remove dirt and dead tissue gently.
  3. Apply the wound treatment and fly repellent your supervisor or vet provides. Fly strike and screw-worm can turn small wounds into big problems.
  4. Check the wound daily until it heals. Call the vet for deep wounds, wounds near joints or eyes, heavy bleeding or wounds that smell or swell.

Dipping and spraying

Plunge dips and spray races are the main ways to control ticks on many farms. Use only registered products under Act 36 of 1947 and follow the label for mixing, replenishment and intervals.

  • Wear overalls, boots, gloves and face protection when mixing concentrate.
  • Mix in a well-ventilated place and never mix with bare hands.
  • Do not dip animals that are tired, hot, thirsty or very young unless the label allows it; let them rest and drink first.
  • Keep the dip tank fenced and children and dogs away.
  • Never empty dip wash near rivers, dams or boreholes.
  • If concentrate splashes on skin or in eyes, wash with plenty of clean water and get medical help, taking the label with you.

Hoof care

Check feet for overgrown hooves, foot rot (smell, rotten tissue between the claws) and stones or thorns. Trim only if you have been trained. Footbaths are used for foot rot in sheep; follow the product label for concentration and time.

Dealing with dead animals

Do not open the carcass of an animal that died suddenly. Report it and wait for instructions. Burn or bury carcasses as the farm and vet direct, away from water.

Key points

  • Read the label for dose, route and withdrawal period before every treatment.
  • Keep vaccines cold and use clean needles.
  • Never dose an animal with its head held high.
  • Wear protective clothing when mixing dips.
  • Record and mark every treated animal.

quiz.question: How should vaccines be carried to the kraal?

options.text: In a cooler box out of the sun

quiz.question: Why should you dose the group at the weight of the heaviest animals?

options.text: To use up the product faster

quiz.question: Why is the neck preferred over the rump for injections in cattle?

options.text: The neck is easier to reach from the bakkie
It avoids damaging valuable meat cuts
The label never mentions the site

quiz.question: What should you do with used needles?

options.text: Recap them by hand and keep them
Put them in a sharps container

quiz.question: Dip concentrate splashes into a worker's eyes. What is the first step?

options.text: Wash with plenty of clean water and get medical help with the label

quiz.question: It is safe to dose a sheep while its head is held high.
Hot, tired and thirsty animals should rest and drink before dipping.
When should you call the vet about a wound? (select all that apply)

options.text: It is deep or near a joint
It is a small scratch that is healing
